 Recall alone insufficient to support auto defect claims 
 James Andersen // November 3, 2026 // 
 -->
 -->
 Listen to this article 
 Summary 
 A Michigan federal judge dismissed nine of 11 plaintiffs from a class action alleging engine defects in certain Ford Escape, Ford Maverick and Lincoln Corsair hybrid vehicles.
 The court found that vehicle ownership alone was insufficient to establish standing without allegations that the recalled engine defect actually affected the plaintiffs’ vehicles.
 Two plaintiffs can proceed with certain claims after alleging specific engine problems: one experienced an engine stall, while another reported an engine fire.
 The court allowed one plaintiff’s Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act and California Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act claims, along with unjust enrichment claims from both remaining plaintiffs.
 A federal judge has dismissed the majority of plaintiffs from a class action alleging engine defects in Ford and Lincoln vehicles, finding they lacked standing because they did not plausibly allege that the defect identified in a recall by Ford Motor Company affected their vehicles.
 The dispute involves alleged defects in certain Ford Escape, Ford Maverick and Lincoln Corsair hybrid vehicles. The plaintiffs are current or former owners of vehicles covered by the recall. Ford moved to dismiss a second amended complaint in February 2025. 
 Judge Stephen J. Murphy III granted the motion in part, concluding that nine of the 11 plaintiffs lacked standing. A few claims still remain: one plaintiff’s claims under the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act and California’s Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act, and unjust enrichment claims from both remaining plaintiffs.
 “[T]he Court concludes that nine of the eleven plaintiffs — those who did not allege that the defect identified in Ford’s recall manifested in their vehicles — do not have standing,” Murphy wrote. “But the two plaintiffs who alleged more than just ownership of a vehicle covered by the recall — [one plaintiff] whose engine stalled and [one plaintiff] whose engine caught fire — alleged a concrete injury traceable to Ford’s conduct.”
 The 26-page decision is Pacheco v. Ford Motor Co. ; MiLW No. 02-111284 . 
 Contrary to public policy? 
 Attorneys from The Miller Law Firm in Rochester were part of the plaintiffs’ team, which also included attorneys from Washington and Arizona. The firm declined to comment.
 Attorneys from Bush Seyferth in Troy represented Ford. Attorney Stephanie A. Douglas said the case runs contrary to public policy because a comprehensive framework already exists to resolve recalls quickly and at no cost to customers. Class actions like this, she said, intrude on that framework and turn recalls into opportunities for economic gain.
 “We are pleased the court recognized that plaintiffs who have a vehicle in a recall population but who have not plausibly alleged there is anything wrong with their vehicles should not be allowed to bring claims on behalf of themselves and other uninjured people,” she said.
 Recalls lead to lawsuits 
 The lawsuit alleges defects in the 2.5-liter hybrid and plug-in hybrid engines used in certain Ford and Lincoln models. Following reports of under-hood smoke and fires, Ford issued a recall in July 2022. In June 2023, the company expanded the recall to include additional vehicles. Under the recall program, Ford offered a one-time preventive replacement for certain vehicles, while others were eligible for defect detection and engine replacement at no cost if needed.
 This case dates to 2022, when the plaintiffs first sued, asserting a nationwide claim under the federal Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act and 22 state-specific claims under the laws of 10 states.
 The case was assigned to a Michigan federal judge, who dismissed it on mootness grounds because of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration-supervised recall process. The plaintiffs appealed and also sought relief from the judgment following Ford’s recall activity in 2023. The 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals remanded the case with instructions to reopen it and allow an amended complaint.
 In January 2025 a second amended complaint naming 16 plaintiffs was filed, which Ford moved to dismiss. The court stayed the case after granting Ford’s motion to compel arbitration of six plaintiffs’ claims pending resolution of an arbitrability issue. Five of those plaintiffs then voluntarily dismissed their claims.
 When an arbitrator determined that Ford could not compel arbitration of the remaining plaintiff’s claims, the court reopened the case, scheduled a hearing and allowed supplemental briefing on the standing issue.
 The eleven plaintiffs at this stage were all current or former owners of vehicles covered by the recall, but only two alleged that the engine defect had manifested itself in their vehicles.
 Majority of plaintiffs lack standing 
 Murphy relied on recent caselaw from the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals and the Eastern District of Michigan holding that a product recall alone does not establish that a particular product is defective.
 Ford’s recall covered 125,322 potentially affected vehicles, but the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration estimated that just 1% had the defect. Given that, the judge concluded that the nine plaintiffs who had not experienced engine problems could not go forward with their claims.
 “Those plaintiffs did not plausibly allege a universal defect because nothing in their complaint makes it plausible that their vehicles are among the 1% of vehicles estimated to be defective,” Murphy wrote.
 The judge also rejected the plaintiffs’ overpayment theory, finding that without plausible allegations that their own vehicles were defective, they could not establish that they had paid more than the vehicles were worth. Their claims were dismissed without prejudice.
 In addition, the court dismissed remaining fraud-based claims because the plaintiffs did not adequately allege that Ford knew about the defect before they purchased their vehicles. Allegations about Ford’s subsequent investigation and recall activity did not establish pre-sale knowledge, and general allegations about pre-launch testing did not show that the testing revealed a safety defect.
 The court did allow two plaintiffs to proceed with their unjust enrichment claims, finding that Ford’s argument that an express warranty barred those claims relied on a warranty that was not included in the complaint or its accompanying documents.
